assignments.raw_value: Advanced practice registered nurses may prescribe and dispense medical, therapeutic, or corrective measures. APRNs with a DEA registration number must register with the controlled substance prescription database. APRNs may prescribe controlled substances under board regulations. Opioid prescriptions may not exceed a seven-day supply for initial prescriptions to adults or any prescription for minors, with exceptions for certain medical conditions.

RNs and LPNs are authorized to administer legend drugs lawfully ordered or prescribed by an authorized practitioner. CRNPs and CNMs may prescribe legend drugs under approved protocols and formulary with collaborating physician. CRNAs may engage in procedural ordering of medications as part of anesthesia plan. CNS may not prescribe drugs of any type.

APRNs with a certificate of prescriptive authority may prescribe drugs in Schedules III-V and, under certain conditions, Schedule II drugs. CRNAs may administer Schedule II drugs during the perioperative, peri-obstetrical, and medical procedure period. CNMs with full practice authority may prescribe Schedules III-V without a collaborative practice agreement.

Registered nurse practitioners and certified nurse midwives may prescribe, administer, and dispense therapeutic measures including legend drugs, medical devices, and controlled substances within their scope. Clinical nurse specialists may prescribe and dispense pharmacological agents subject to requirements and limits. CRNAs may issue medication orders including controlled substances in specified settings. CNSs have restricted opioid schedule II prescribing. Board may adopt rules prohibiting NPs, CNSs, and CNMs from dispensing schedule II opioids except for specified exceptions.

Registered nurses may administer medications and therapeutic agents as ordered by a licensed physician, dentist, podiatrist, or clinical psychologist. Nurse practitioners with a furnishing number may furnish/order Schedule II-V controlled substances under standardized procedures or independently under Section 2837.103. Certified nurse-midwives with a furnishing number may furnish/order Schedule II-V controlled substances within their scope. Nurse anesthetists may select and administer medication including controlled substances for anesthesia services pursuant to a physician/dentist/podiatrist

APRNs with prescriptive authority may prescribe controlled substances and prescription drugs within their scope of practice and role/population focus; prescriptive authority requires board approval and mentorship. An APRN with prescriptive authority is subject to the 7-day opioid prescribing limit for new patients and electronic prescribing requirements for controlled substances.

APRNs may prescribe, dispense and administer medical therapeutics and corrective measures including controlled substances in schedules II, III, IV, and V. For the first three years after licensure, an APRN must collaborate with a physician; thereafter, an APRN may prescribe independently after meeting the required 3-year/2,000-hour threshold. CRNAs certified by AANA may prescribe, dispense and administer drugs including controlled substances in schedule II, III, IV, or V.

An APRN licensed by the Board may prescribe, order, procure, administer, store, dispense and furnish over the counter, legend and controlled substances pursuant to applicable state and federal laws and within the APRN's role and population focus.

RNs and LPNs may administer medications and treatments as prescribed by a duly licensed practitioner. APRNs may prescribe, dispense, administer, or order any drug within an established supervisory protocol; controlled substances may be prescribed only by APRNs with a master's or doctoral degree in a clinical nursing specialty with training in specialized practitioner skills. Schedule II controlled substances are limited to a 7-day supply except for psychiatric medications prescribed by psychiatric nurses. APRNs in autonomous practice may prescribe within primary care scope.

Registered professional nurses may administer medications and treatments as prescribed by a physician, dentist, or podiatrist; may administer, order, and dispense medications, diagnostic studies, and medical treatments authorized by protocol when authorized by other general laws. APRNs may prescribe pursuant to nurse protocol agreement under Code Section 43-34-25.

APRNs with prescriptive authority may prescribe and administer over the counter drugs, legend drugs, and controlled substances; prescribe, order, and dispense medical devices and equipment. An exclusionary formulary is determined by the board.

An ARNP may prescribe substances or devices, including controlled substances or devices, if the nurse is engaged in the practice of a nursing specialty regulated under rules adopted by the board of nursing in consultation with the board of medicine and the board of pharmacy. An RN may supply prescription drugs, controlled substances, or contraceptive devices on direct order of supervising physician when pharmacist services are not reasonably available.
APRNs may prescribe, administer and dispense therapeutic pharmacologic agents as defined by board rules. RNs and LPNs may administer medications as prescribed by authorized health care providers.

APRNs with a written collaborative agreement may be delegated authority to prescribe Schedule III-V controlled substances and, under specific conditions, Schedule II by oral/topical/transdermal routes. APRNs with full practice authority may prescribe Schedule II-V controlled substances; Schedule II narcotic drugs (e.g., opioids) only in a consultation relationship with a physician. APRNs in hospitals/hospital affiliates may be privileged to prescribe Schedule II-V controlled substances. CRNAs may select, order, and administer medication including controlled substances for anesthesia services u

Advanced practice registered nurses (excluding CRNAs) may be authorized by the board to prescribe drugs, including controlled substances, subject to board rules, a practice agreement, and continuing education requirements. CRNAs may administer anesthesia under the direction of and in the immediate presence of a physician without requiring separate prescriptive authority.

An APRN may prescribe durable medical equipment and prescribe, procure and administer any drug consistent with the licensee's specific role and population focus, except no drug intended to cause an abortion. Controlled substances must be prescribed in accordance with the uniform controlled substances act and require DEA registration. APRNs may not dispense drugs but may request, receive and sign for professional samples.

APRNs may issue prescriptions for and dispense nonscheduled legend drugs, and issue prescriptions for (but not dispense) Schedules II-V controlled substances under conditions set forth in KRS 314.042, including CAPA-NS and CAPA-CS requirements. CRNAs are exempt from prescriptive authority requirements for anesthesia care.

APRNs may prescribe legend and certain controlled drugs, therapeutic regimens, medical devices, and appliances under a collaborative practice agreement. RNs may not prescribe drugs but may execute health care regimens as prescribed by authorized prescribers. CRNAs may administer anesthetics and medications necessary for anesthesia care under physician/dentist direction and supervision.

Advanced practice nurses (NPs, CRNAs, CNMs, PNMHCS) may issue written prescriptions and medication orders and order therapeutics pursuant to guidelines mutually developed with a supervising provider, or independently after 2 years supervised practice following certification. Nurse anesthetists do not require prescriptive authority to deliver anesthesia care.

Nurse practitioners and nurse midwives may prescribe drugs including controlled substances on Schedules II-V. Nurse anesthetists may prescribe drugs including controlled dangerous substances for up to a 10-day supply in connection with anesthesia services. Clinical nurse specialists may prescribe drugs under Board regulations. Registered nurses may prepare and dispense drugs in limited public health settings.

A certified nurse practitioner or a certified nurse midwife who qualifies as an advanced practice registered nurse may prescribe and dispense drugs or devices, or both, in accordance with rules adopted by the board. CRNAs in critical access hospitals and rural hospitals may order and prescribe prescription drugs in the preoperative and immediate postoperative period, with controlled substance prescribing limited to Schedules III, IIIN, IV and V for up to 4 days with no refills.

APRNs may prescribe nonscheduled prescription drugs and, as a delegated act of a physician, controlled substances included in schedules 2 to 5. Nurse anesthetists may select, order, prescribe, and administer anesthesia and analgesic agents including controlled substances within defined perioperative/periobstetrical/periprocedural scope. RNs may receive delegated authority to order, receive, and dispense complimentary starter dose drugs (non-controlled) from a supervising physician.

Advanced practice registered nurses are authorized to prescribe, procure, sign for, record, administer, and dispense over-the-counter, legend, and controlled substances, including sample drugs. APRNs must comply with DEA requirements for controlled substances. Registered nurses may implement prescribing protocols delegated by a licensed practitioner.

APRNs may prescribe, dispense, and administer medications and nonscheduled legend drugs within their practice and specialty. With a certificate of controlled substance prescriptive authority, APRNs may also prescribe controlled substances under a collaborative practice arrangement with a physician with an unrestricted DEA registration.

RNs and LPNs may administer medications and treatments prescribed by a licensed physician or dentist. APRNs (CNMs and CNPs) may apply for controlled substance prescriptive authority (Schedules II-V) after completing a board-approved educational program. CRNAs collaborate with physicians/dentists but do not have general prescriptive authority under the statute. Nurse practitioners may not write prescriptions for, dispense or order controlled substances except as contained in this chapter.

RNs may administer medications and treatments prescribed by physicians, naturopathic physicians, physician assistants, optometrists, advanced practice registered nurses, dentists, osteopaths, or podiatrists. APRNs may have prescriptive authority upon board approval.

RNs may implement the treatment and pharmaceutical regimen prescribed by any person authorized by State law to prescribe the regimen; subject to G.S. 90-18.2, RNs may not prescribe a medical treatment regimen or make a medical diagnosis except under supervision of a licensed physician.

Nurses may administer medications (including by parenteral route for licensed nurses); APRNs have prescriptive practices defined as assessing the need for drugs, immunizing agents, or devices and writing a prescription to be filled by a licensed pharmacist. Delegation of medication administration to unlicensed persons (non-parenteral) is authorized under specific settings.

Nurse practitioners may prescribe therapeutic measures and medications within their scope of practice. CRNAs administer anesthesia. LPNs and RNs execute regimens prescribed by authorized prescribers. NPs may prescribe controlled substances subject to applicable requirements.

An APRN shall have plenary authority to possess, compound, prescribe, administer, and dispense and distribute to clients controlled and non-controlled drugs within the scope of the APRN's practice. APRNs may prescribe non-opioid and opioid controlled drugs classified in schedule II through IV, including by telemedicine.

Advanced practice nurses may prescribe or order medications and devices in inpatient and outpatient settings pursuant to joint protocols developed with a collaborating physician, including controlled dangerous substances. APNs may also dispense narcotic drugs for maintenance or detoxification treatment if they meet federal training and registration requirements. RNs and LPNs execute medical regimens as prescribed by a physician or dentist.

RNs may administer medications and treatments prescribed by authorized persons, and may administer anesthetics up to and including moderate sedation upon completion of required training. CNPs, CRNAs, and CNSs with prescriptive authority may prescribe and distribute dangerous drugs and controlled substances in Schedules II-V within their respective scopes.

RNs administer medications and treatments as prescribed by authorized practitioners. APRNs may prescribe controlled substances, poisons, dangerous drugs and devices if authorized pursuant to NRS 639.2351; may not prescribe Schedule II controlled substances unless they have at least 2 years or 2,000 hours of clinical experience, or the substance is prescribed pursuant to a protocol approved by a collaborating physician. CRNAs may, under physician supervision in a critical access hospital, order, prescribe, possess and administer controlled substances, poisons, dangerous drugs and devices for su

Nurse practitioners may issue prescriptions for drugs, devices and immunizing agents in accordance with practice agreement and practice protocols; CNPs with 3,600+ hours may prescribe under alternative collaborative relationship model; NPs may prescribe non-patient specific regimens to RNs and pharmacists for specified purposes; CNPs must obtain a prescribing certificate after completing pharmacology component.

RNs may administer medications and treatments as authorized by a licensed practitioner. APRNs designated as CNS, CNM, or CNP may prescribe drugs and therapeutic devices subject to a standard care arrangement and the exclusionary formulary; prescribing of schedule II controlled substances is subject to restrictions. CRNAs do not independently prescribe but administer anesthesia under physician/podiatrist/dentist supervision.

APRNs (CNP, CNS, CNM) may obtain prescriptive authority recognized by the Board; CRNAs may order, select, obtain, and administer legend drugs and Schedules II-V controlled substances during perioperative/periobstetrical period in collaboration with a physician; CNPs, CNSs, and CNMs may obtain independent prescriptive authority after 6,240 supervised clinical hours.

Nurse practitioners and clinical nurse specialists may be authorized to write prescriptions including controlled substances listed in schedules II through V. CRNAs may prescribe prescription drugs including controlled substances listed in Schedules II, III, III N, IV and V.

CRNPs may prescribe and dispense categories of drugs authorized by board regulations if acting in collaboration with a physician under a written agreement and having completed at least 45 hours of advanced pharmacology coursework. Drug categories are subject to approval by the Drug Review Committee. CRNAs may administer anesthesia under overall direction of a qualified physician, podiatrist, or dentist. CNSs may not prescribe medical therapeutic or corrective measures.

APRNs licensed by the board may prescribe, order, procure, administer, dispense, and furnish over-the-counter, legend, and controlled substances (Schedules II-V for CNPs; limited schedules for psychiatric/mental health APRNs; CRNAs per chapter 34.2). Prescriptive authority is granted by the board of nursing.

APRNs (NP, CNM, CNS) with prescriptive authority may prescribe medications including Schedules III-V controlled substances and Schedule II nonnarcotic substances (up to 30-day supply) and Schedule II narcotic substances (up to 5-day supply, with physician agreement, or up to 30-day supply for hospice/palliative/long-term care patients), pursuant to a practice agreement. CRNAs do not require prescriptive authority to deliver anesthesia care.

CRNAs may prescribe, procure, administer, and furnish pharmacological agents including controlled drugs listed on Schedule II in connection with anesthesia practice or pain management. CNPs and CNMs may prescribe, procure, administer, and furnish pharmacological agents including over the counter, legend, and controlled drugs listed on Schedule II. CNSs may, in collaboration with a licensed physician, order and dispense durable medical equipment or therapeutic devices.

Nurse practitioners with a certificate of fitness may prescribe and/or issue legend drugs within formulary limitations and, upon joint adoption of physician collaboration rules, may prescribe controlled substances in Schedules II, III, IV, and V, subject to formulary and collaboration requirements. CRNAs may select, order, or administer drugs within their scope during services ordered by a physician, dentist, or podiatrist.

RNs may administer medications as ordered by a physician, podiatrist, or dentist. APRNs may request, receive, sign for, and distribute prescription drug samples at authorized practices, and may prescribe or order drugs or devices as delegated by a physician under a prescriptive authority agreement. APRNs must complete pharmacology and pathophysiology education and obtain a board-issued prescription authorization number.

APRNs may prescribe or administer prescription drugs or devices including local anesthesia, Schedule III-V controlled substances, and Schedule II controlled substances (except CRNAs in anesthesia practice, who administer anesthetics and adjunct drugs and fluids as part of anesthesia care). Medication aides certified may administer routine medications by specified routes in long-term care facilities under licensed nurse supervision.

RNs and LPNs may administer medications and treatments as prescribed by any person authorized by law to prescribe. APRNs are jointly licensed by the Boards of Medicine and Nursing and may prescribe within their scope.
APRNs are authorized to perform acts of medical diagnosis and to prescribe medical, therapeutic, or corrective measures under administrative rules adopted by the Board.

Advanced registered nurse practitioners/advanced practice registered nurses may prescribe legend drugs and controlled substances in Schedules II–V upon board approval, subject to limitations. CRNAs may select, order, or administer Schedules II–IV controlled substances for anesthesia. Schedule I controlled substances are prohibited.

APRNs may issue prescription orders subject to board rules, including controlled substances; they may prescribe opioid antagonists and provide expedited partner therapy. Board rules specify classes of drugs that may not be prescribed. APRNs without a prescription notation may not issue prescription orders.

APRNs may prescribe drugs under a collaborative agreement; may prescribe up to a 3-day supply of Schedule II narcotics; may not prescribe Schedule I controlled substances; after 3 years in documented collaborative relationship with prescriptive authority, may prescribe without collaborative agreement. Prescriptive authority must be renewed biennially.

APRNs may prescribe, administer, dispense or provide nonprescriptive and prescriptive medications including prepackaged medications, except schedule I drugs. For licensees with prescriptive authority, 3 hours of CE on controlled substance prescribing required biennially.

assignments.raw_value: An APRN may not issue an initial prescription for an opioid exceeding a seven-day supply to an adult for outpatient use, or any opioid prescription exceeding a seven-day supply to a minor, with exceptions for certain medical conditions or logistical barriers.

APRNs may prescribe Schedule II opioids only for a five-day period or less. The board shall promulgate rules limiting the amount of Schedule II narcotics that may be prescribed and dispensed by licensees.

Board may adopt rules prohibiting registered nurse practitioners, clinical nurse specialists or certified nurse midwives from dispensing a schedule II controlled substance that is an opioid, except for an implantable device or an opioid for medication-assisted treatment for substance use disorders or as provided in section 32-3248.03. CNSs in hospital settings may not prescribe schedule II opioids except pursuant to institutional protocols or standing orders.

APRNs with prescriptive authority are subject to the 7-day supply limit for opioids for patients who have not obtained an opioid prescription from that prescriber within the last 12 months, with exceptions for chronic pain, cancer, post-surgical pain expected to last more than 14 days, and palliative/hospice care.

The formulary must also limit the prescribing of Schedule II controlled substances as listed in s. 893.03 to a 7-day supply, except that such restriction does not apply to controlled substances that are psychiatric medications prescribed by psychiatric nurses.

APRNs with full practice authority may prescribe Schedule II narcotic drugs (such as opioids) only in a consultation relationship with a physician; specific drug must be identified by brand or generic name; only by oral dosage or topical/transdermal application (not injection); at least monthly the APRN and physician must discuss patients for whom an opioid is prescribed.

Schedule II controlled substances (except hydrocodone combination products) limited to 72-hour supply without refill; hydrocodone combination products limited to 30-day supply without refill; Schedule III limited to 30-day supply without refill; Schedules IV and V limited to original prescription and refills not to exceed 6-month supply.

Nurse anesthetists may only prescribe in amounts not exceeding a 10-day supply, only for individuals with whom the nurse anesthetist has established a client or patient record at the time of prescription, and only in connection with the delivery of anesthesia services.

APRNs and others with prescribing authority may not prescribe more than 100 MME per day in aggregate, not more than a 30-day supply for chronic pain within a 30-day period (on/after Jan 1, 2017), and not more than a 7-day supply for acute pain within a 7-day period (on/after Jan 1, 2017). CRNAs in critical access/rural hospitals may prescribe controlled substances (Schedules III, IIIN, IV, V) for no more than 4 days with no refills.

When prescribing opioids to opioid-naive patients on an outpatient basis, the prescription may not be for more than a 7-day supply, with exceptions for chronic pain, cancer pain, palliative care, or opioid abuse treatment.

APRNs may prescribe opioid controlled drugs classified in schedule II through IV by telemedicine after establishing an APRN-patient relationship; a subsequent in-person exam shall be conducted at intervals appropriate for the patient, medical condition, and drug, but not less than annually.

APNs must complete six contact hours of CE in pharmacology related to controlled substances including prescription opioid drugs. Prescribing of Schedule II controlled dangerous substances via telemedicine requires initial in-person examination and subsequent in-person visit every three months.

APRNs registered to dispense controlled substances must complete at least 2 hours of training relating to persons with substance use or other addictive disorders and the prescribing of opioids during each period of licensure. APRNs may not prescribe Schedule II controlled substances unless they have at least 2 years or 2,000 hours of clinical experience, or the controlled substance is prescribed pursuant to a protocol approved by a collaborating physician.

Must comply with section 3719.061 before issuing a prescription for an opioid analgesic to a minor. Must check the drug database before prescribing opioid analgesics or benzodiazepines and reassess every 90 days.

APRNs with prescriptive authority are prohibited from prescribing opioid drugs in excess of the maximum limits authorized in Section 2-309I of Title 63 of the Oklahoma Statutes; CE renewal requires 2 hours of education in pain management or opioid use/addiction.

Schedule II narcotic substances: prescription must not exceed a five-day supply and another prescription must not be written without written agreement of the physician, unless for patients in hospice or palliative care or residing in long-term care facilities, in which case each prescription must not exceed a thirty-day supply.

A nurse practitioner who has been issued a certificate of fitness may only prescribe or issue a Schedule II or III opioid listed on the formulary for a maximum of a non-refillable, thirty-day course of treatment unless specifically approved after consultation with the collaborating physician before the initial issuance of the prescription or dispensing of the medication. This does not apply to prescriptions issued in a hospital, a nursing home licensed under title 68, or inpatient facilities licensed under title 33.

By January 1, 2019, the board must adopt rules establishing requirements for prescribing opioid drugs. By January 1, 2020, the board must require APRNs who prescribe opioids to inform patients of their right to refuse an opioid prescription.

APRN may prescribe up to a three-day supply of a Schedule II narcotic; exception for APRNs participating in a clinical trial with IRB approval for rural expansion of medication-assisted treatment for opioid use disorder.

assignments.raw_value: APRNs may prescribe non-controlled substances without a physical examination if follow-up care is available and records are sent to the primary care provider with patient consent. Controlled substances may also be prescribed if these requirements are met. APRNs may not prescribe in response to an Internet questionnaire or email to a person with whom they lack a prior provider-patient relationship.

Healthcare services provided by telemedicine, including a prescription through telemedicine, shall be held to the same standard of care as healthcare services provided in person. A professional relationship must be established prior to providing telemedicine services.
Any APRN rendering services in person or by electronic means in Delaware must hold an active Delaware RN and APRN license.

A telehealth provider may not use telehealth to prescribe a controlled substance listed in Schedule II of s. 893.03 unless prescribed for: treatment of a psychiatric disorder; inpatient treatment at a licensed hospital; treatment of a patient receiving hospice services; or treatment of a resident of a nursing home facility.

Services relating to the practice of nursing provided by telehealth shall be consistent with all federal and state privacy, security, and confidentiality laws. The board shall develop and adopt rules as necessary relating to the practice of nursing in telehealth.

A provider may issue prescription drug orders via virtual care within the scope of the provider's license, but controlled substances may not be prescribed unless in compliance with 21 U.S.C. Treatment based solely on a static online questionnaire does not constitute an acceptable standard of care.

Temporary permits for APRNs from other states authorize practice 'at the location or locations specified on the permit or via telehealth.' Full practice authority APRNs may practice via telehealth under their permit location or telehealth.

A treating nurse who provides or facilitates the use of telehealth shall ensure informed consent and confidentiality; the board shall promulgate regulations to prevent abuse, fraud, and fee-splitting through telehealth.

A person licensed under this chapter may provide telehealth services as long as the licensee acts within the scope of practice of the licensee's license, in accordance with any requirements and restrictions imposed by this subchapter and in accordance with standards of practice. All laws and rules governing professional responsibility, unprofessional conduct and generally accepted standards of practice apply while providing telehealth services.

A health professional providing telehealth services may prescribe drugs if acting within scope of practice; controlled substance prescribing must meet applicable statutory requirements. No prior in-person examination requirement is stated but the prescriber must be a prescriber acting within scope.

APRNs providing services under a collaborative practice arrangement may provide such services outside the geographic proximity requirements if the collaborating physician and APRN utilize telehealth. Telehealth providers must obtain patient consent before telehealth services are initiated and ensure confidentiality of medical information.

A person licensed under Title 37 to provide health care may provide services by means of telehealth when appropriate for services being provided, meets standard of care, and complies with board administrative rules for telehealth.

An APRN licensed under this chapter may prescribe non-opioid and opioid controlled drugs classified in schedule II through IV by means of telemedicine after establishing an APRN-patient relationship. A subsequent in-person exam shall be conducted at intervals appropriate for the patient, medical condition, and drug, but not less than annually.

APNs may provide health care via telemedicine/telehealth; must be validly licensed/certified, subject to NJ licensing board regulation, maintain liability insurance, and subject to NJ jurisdiction. Schedule II controlled dangerous substances may only be prescribed via telemedicine after an initial in-person examination, with in-person visits required every three months thereafter.

An APRN may perform diagnosis, treatment, and prescribing by using equipment that transfers information concerning the medical condition of a patient in this State electronically, telephonically or by fiber optics, including through telehealth, from within or outside this State or the United States.

APRNs may provide telehealth services. A board may require an initial in-person visit prior to prescribing a schedule II controlled substance to a new patient, but not for hospice/palliative care, medication-assisted treatment, mental health conditions, or emergency situations.

An APRN may perform medical acts via telemedicine pursuant to a practice agreement without being licensed to practice medicine in SC. An APRN may not establish a nurse-patient relationship by telemedicine for the purpose of prescribing medication when an in-person physical examination is necessary for diagnosis. Schedule II-V prescriptions via telemedicine are only permitted pursuant to a practice agreement, and telemedicine prescribing otherwise restricted by Section 40-47-37(C)(6) requires joint committee approval.

An APRN with a certificate of fitness who provides services at a remote site may arrange for required personal review of charts by a collaborating physician via HIPAA-compliant electronic means or in person. Up to 10 required annual remote site visits by a collaborating physician may be conducted by HIPAA-compliant electronic means rather than in person.

The Texas Board of Nursing, Texas Medical Board, Texas Physician Assistant Board, and Texas State Board of Pharmacy shall jointly adopt rules establishing the determination of a valid prescription for telemedicine services. APRNs providing telehealth services are subject to the same standard of care as in-person services.

An APRN may not prescribe medication in response to communication transmitted electronically without verifying patient identity, establishing a documented diagnosis through accepted medical practices, and maintaining a current medical record. An electronic, online, or telephonic evaluation by questionnaire is inadequate for initial evaluation, with specified exceptions.

Telehealth practice is regulated; health care practitioners including nurses may provide telehealth services. A prohibition on prescribing Schedule II controlled substances via telehealth applies unless authorized otherwise. An established patient must visit an in-person practitioner within 12 months of initial telehealth service, with exceptions.
